claim: Trafficking of myelin-reactive CD4+ T-cells across the brain endothelium is an essential step in the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis (MS).
source: Trafficking of myelin-reactive CD4+ T-cells across the brain endothelium, an essential step in the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis (MS), is suggested to be an antigen-specific process, yet which cells provide this signal is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, drawing from the scientific understanding of MS pathogenesis.

claim: Trafficking of myelin-reactive CD4+ T-cells across the brain endothelium is suggested to be an antigen-specific process.
source: Trafficking of myelin-reactive CD4+ T-cells across the brain endothelium, an essential step in the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis (MS), is suggested to be an antigen-specific process, yet which cells provide this signal is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior studies mentioned in the introduction, though the specific citations are not in this sentence.

claim: Under inflammatory conditions, brain endothelial cells (BECs) stimulate the migration of myelin-reactive CD4+ T-cells by acting as non-professional antigen presenting cells through the processing and presentation of myelin-derived antigens in MHC-II.
source: Here we provide direct evidence that under inflammatory conditions, brain endothelial cells (BECs) stimulate the migration of myelin-reactive CD4+ T-cells by acting as non-professional antigen presenting cells through the processing and presentation of myelin-derived antigens in MHC-II.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inflamed BECs internalized myelin, which was routed to endo-lysosomal compartment for processing in a time-dependent manner.
source: Inflamed BECs internalized myelin, which was routed to endo-lysosomal compartment for processing in a time-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Myelin/MHC-II complexes on inflamed BECs stimulated the trans-endothelial migration of myelin-reactive Th1 and Th17 2D2 cells.
source: Moreover, myelin/MHC-II complexes on inflamed BECs stimulated the trans-endothelial migration of myelin-reactive Th1 and Th17 2D2 cells, while control antigen loaded BECs did not stimulate T-cell migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Control antigen loaded BECs did not stimulate T-cell migration.
source: Moreover, myelin/MHC-II complexes on inflamed BECs stimulated the trans-endothelial migration of myelin-reactive Th1 and Th17 2D2 cells, while control antigen loaded BECs did not stimulate T-cell migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Blocking the interaction between myelin/MHC-II complexes and myelin-reactive T-cells prevented T-cell transmigration.
source: Furthermore, blocking the interaction between myelin/MHC-II complexes and myelin-reactive T-cells prevented T-cell transmigration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Endothelial cells derived from the brain are capable of enhancing antigen-specific T cell recruitment.
source: These results demonstrate that endothelial cells derived from the brain are capable of enhancing antigen-specific T cell recruitment.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Once within the central nervous system (CNS), myelin-reactive T-cells induce severe neuronal and tissue damage and degeneration.
source: Once within the central nervous system (CNS), myelin-reactive T-cells induce severe neuronal and tissue damage and degeneration (Trapp et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trapp et al., 1998.

claim: During the initiation of MS disease, myelin-specific CD4+ T cells are differentiated into effector T helper (Th) 1 or Th17 cells.
source: During the initiation of the disease, myelin-specific CD4+ T cells are differentiated into effector T helper (Th) 1 or Th17 cells (Bailey et al., 2007; Bielekova et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bailey et al., 2007 and Bielekova et al., 2000.

claim: Th1 and Th17 cells, separately or in cooperation, mediate deleterious responses in MS.
source: There is compelling evidence that Th1 and Th17 cells, separately or in cooperation, mediate deleterious responses in MS (Carbajal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carbajal et al., 2015.

claim: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is composed of highly specialized brain endothelial cells (BECs) that are sealed by closely regulated tight junctions.
source: To enter the CNS, immune cells have to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which is composed of highly specialized brain endothelial cells (BECs) that are sealed by closely regulated tight junctions (Tietz and Engelhardt, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tietz and Engelhardt, 2015.

claim: Lymphocyte migration into the CNS parenchyma is a multi-step process that requires close contact between lymphocytes and BECs.
source: Lymphocyte migration into the CNS parenchyma is a multi-step process that requires close contact between lymphocytes and BECs (Ransohoff et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ransohoff et al., 2003.

claim: During inflammation BECs upregulate the expression of the adhesion molecules Inter-Cellular Adhesion Molecule (ICAM)−1, Vascular cell adhesion molecule (VCAM)−1 and Activated leukocyte cell adhesion molecule (ALCAM).
source: During inflammation BECs upregulate the expression of the adhesion molecules Inter-Cellular Adhesion Molecule (ICAM)−1, Vascular cell adhesion molecule (VCAM)−1 and Activated leukocyte cell adhesion molecule (ALCAM), which are necessary for the firm adhesion of lymphocytes to the endothelium as well as for the trans-migration process (Larochelle et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Larochelle et al., 2011.

claim: ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and ALCAM are necessary for the firm adhesion of lymphocytes to the endothelium as well as for the trans-migration process.
source: During inflammation BECs upregulate the expression of the adhesion molecules Inter-Cellular Adhesion Molecule (ICAM)−1, Vascular cell adhesion molecule (VCAM)−1 and Activated leukocyte cell adhesion molecule (ALCAM), which are necessary for the firm adhesion of lymphocytes to the endothelium as well as for the trans-migration process (Larochelle et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Larochelle et al., 2011.

claim: Only activated myelin-specific CD4+ T-cells accumulated in the CNS parenchyma, while non-CNS-specific T-cells failed to infiltrate in an adoptive transfer model of murine MS (EAE).
source: Using an adoptive transfer model of murine MS (experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, EAE) it was demonstrated that only activated myelin-specific CD4+ T-cells accumulated in the CNS parenchyma, while non-CNS-specific T-cells failed to infiltrate (Archambault et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Archambault et al., 2005.

claim: Expression of MHC-II on the recipient cells appeared to be required for CNS infiltration, as the myelin-specific T-cells did not transmigrate over CNS vascular endothelium when adoptively transferred in MHC-II deficient mice.
source: Furthermore, expression of MHC-II on the recipient cells appeared to be required for CNS infiltration, as the myelin-specific T-cells did not transmigrate over CNS vascular endothelium when adoptively transferred in MHC-II deficient mice.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from prior studies, as indicated by the context referencing Archambault et al., 2005.

claim: Infiltration of CD8+ T-cells into the brain was shown to be an antigen-specific process: haemagglutinin-specific CD8+ T-cells were only detected in the CNS upon intra-cerebral injection of cognate, but not control, peptides in an haemagglutinin T-cell receptor transgenic mouse.
source: Also infiltration of CD8+ T-cells into the brain was shown to be an antigen-specific process: haemagglutinin-specific CD8+ T-cells were only detected in the CNS upon intra-cerebral injection of cognate, but not control, peptides in an haemagglutinin T-cell receptor transgenic mouse (Galea et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Galea et al., 2007.

claim: Luminal expression of MHC-I on BECs was observed.
source: A role for BECs in providing the antigen signal to T-cells was claimed by showing luminal expression of MHC-I on BECs and the fact that intra-venous injection of a blocking MHC-I antibody significantly reduced the CD8+ T-cell infiltration.
evidence: This claim is based on prior studies referenced in the context of Galea et al., 2007.

claim: Intra-venous injection of a blocking MHC-I antibody significantly reduced the CD8+ T-cell infiltration.
source: A role for BECs in providing the antigen signal to T-cells was claimed by showing luminal expression of MHC-I on BECs and the fact that intra-venous injection of a blocking MHC-I antibody significantly reduced the CD8+ T-cell infiltration.
evidence: This claim is based on prior studies referenced in the context of Galea et al., 2007.

claim: BECs have been shown to express MHC-I while MHC-II is virtually absent.
source: BECs have been shown to express MHC-I while MHC-II is virtually absent.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inflammation induced activation of BECs causes increased expression of MHC-II as well as of the co-stimulatory molecule CD40 and enhanced their ability to stimulate the proliferation of allogeneic T-cells in-vitro.
source: Inflammation induced activation of BECs causes increased expression of MHC-II as well as of the co-stimulatory molecule CD40 and enhanced their ability to stimulate the proliferation of allogeneic T-cells in-vitro (Wheway et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wheway et al., 2013.

claim: BECs have been shown to take up soluble antigens by macro-pinocytosis and clathrin-coated pits.
source: Although BECs have been shown to take up soluble antigens by macro-pinocytosis and clathrin-coated pits (Wheway et al., 2013), not much is known about their capacity to process and present internalized antigens.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wheway et al., 2013.

claim: Resting, non-inflamed, human BECs express MHC-I and PD-L1 while MHC-II, CD40 and VCAM−1 are expressed at low levels.
source: Resting, non-inflamed, human BECs express MHC-I and PD-L1 while MHC-II, CD40 and VCAM−1 are expressed at low levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Upon inflammatory activation, BECs express high levels of VCAM−1, and significantly increased the expression levels of MHC-II.
source: Upon inflammatory activation, BECs express high levels of VCAM−1, and significantly increased the expression levels of MHC-II (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: CD40 expression was increased upon activation of BECs.
source: Similarly, CD40 expression was increased upon activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both MHC-I and PD-L1 were highly expressed on resting as well as on activated BECs.
source: Both MHC-I and PD-L1 were highly expressed on resting as well as on activated BECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of the classical co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 were undetectable on resting and activated BECs.
source: Expression of the classical co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 were undetectable on resting and activated BECs (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data mentioned but not shown.

claim: Up-regulation of MHC class II molecules via inflammation induced CIITA activity has been associated with increased susceptibility of EAE.
source: Up-regulation of MHC class II molecules via inflammation induced CIITA activity has been associated with increased susceptibility of EAE, yet how increased MHC-II expression contributes to actual disease has so far not been described (Reith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reith et al., 2005.

claim: A time-dependent increase in the proportion of myelin+ BECs was observed.
source: As depicted in Figure 1C a time-dependent increase in the proportion of myelin+ BECs was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Myelin uptake by BECs is not significantly affected by treatment with inflammatory stimuli as activated BECs showed a similar amount of internalized myelin as resting BECs.
source: Moreover, this process is not significantly affected by treatment with inflammatory stimuli as activated BECs showed a similar amount of internalized myelin as resting BECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: BECs that were able to capture myelin increased the number of myelin particles over time to a maximum of three myelin particles/cell after a 24 hr incubation.
source: Using imaging flow cytometry, we assessed that BECs that were able to capture myelin increased the number of myelin particles over time to a maximum of three myelin particles/cell after a 24 hr incubation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The average amount of myelin particles per cell was the same in both resting and inflammatory conditions.
source: Moreover, the average amount of myelin particles per cell was the same in both resting and inflammatory conditions, again, demonstrating that this process is not significantly affected by treatment with inflammatory stimuli (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: The myelin fluorescence signal was intracellular, demonstrating that BECs are able to efficiently internalize myelin.
source: The results indicate that the myelin fluorescence signal was intracellular, demonstrating that BECs are able to efficiently internalize myelin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The endo-lysosomes are the typical antigen-processing compartments of APCs.
source: The endo-lysosomes are the typical antigen-processing compartments of APCs (Blum et al., 2013; Roche and Furuta, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blum et al., 2013 and Roche and Furuta, 2015.

claim: Myelin co-localized with both EEA1 and LAMP1 as shown by a high co-localization score.
source: We observed that myelin co-localized with both EEA1 and LAMP1 as shown by a high co-localization score (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The co-localization with both EEA1 and LAMP1 markers was higher at 24 hr of exposure to myelin compared to 4 hr.
source: The co-localization with both markers was higher at 24 hr of exposure to myelin compared to 4 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: At 24 hr the majority of myelin was present in lysosomes.
source: Since the increase of the co-localization score for myelin-EEA1 was not as strong as shown for myelin-LAMP1 at 24 hr (Figure 2A,B), this suggests that at that time point the majority of myelin was present in lysosomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential co-localization scores shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: 24 hr after loading of adherent BECs a proportion of cells show internalized myelin.
source: Similar to our experiments using imaging flow cytometry, we observe that 24 hr after loading of adherent BECs a proportion of cells show internalized myelin.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2C-I.

claim: Internalized myelin is present within LAMP1 positive vesicles and not with EEA1 positive organelles.
source: Furthermore, it is clear that internalized myelin is present within LAMP1 positive vesicles and not with EEA1 positive organelles (Figure 2C–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2C-I.

claim: Myelin enters the endosomal/lysosomal pathway when internalized by BECs.
source: Together, these data suggest that myelin enters the endosomal/lysosomal pathway when internalized by BECs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The efficiency of myelin uptake and internal routing to compartments associated with antigen processing by BECs is not affected by inflammation per se.
source: Furthermore, it is clear that the efficiency of myelin uptake and internal routing to compartments associated with antigen processing by BECs is not affected by inflammation per se.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Only in an immature state DCs possess high antigen internalization and processing capacities.
source: This is in contrast to their professional counterparts: only in an immature state DCs possess high antigen internalization and processing capacities.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dendritic cells.

claim: Activation induced maturation of DCs strongly reduces antigen internalization and processing functions, and increases the presentation of antigens in MHC molecules.
source: Activation induced maturation of DCs strongly reduces these functions, and increases the presentation of antigens in MHC molecules (Inaba et al., 2000; Jin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Inaba et al., 2000 and Jin et al., 2004.

claim: An increased expression of MHC-II was observed on cerebral blood vessels of mice in the active phase of EAE when compared to control adjuvant injected mice (CFA).
source: Notably, an increased expression of MHC-II was observed on cerebral blood vessels of mice in the active phase of EAE when compared to control adjuvant injected mice (CFA; not shown), demonstrating that mBECs, similar to the human counterparts, are properly equipped to present antigens to pathogenic CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data mentioned but not shown.

claim: In the brain of MS patients and of EAE mice mainly Th1 and Th17 effector cells have been found.
source: Since in the brain of MS patients and of EAE mice mainly Th1 and Th17 effector cells have been found (Carbajal et al., 2015), we generated MOG-specific Th1 and Th17 in-vitro (Figure 3A) and used them in a trans-well setting with myelin-loaded activated mBECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carbajal et al., 2015.

claim: Loading of mBECs with OVA did not significantly induce the migration of any of the MOG-specific T-cell subsets, similar to medium-control mBECs.
source: Loading of mBECs with OVA did not significantly induce the migration of any of the MOG-specific T-cell subsets, similar to medium-control mBECs (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: When mBECs were loaded with myelin, a significant increase in migrated Th1 and Th17 cells was observed.
source: However, when mBECs were loaded with myelin, a significant increase in migrated Th1 and Th17 cells was observed, demonstrating that processing and presentation of myelin-derived peptides by mBECs specifically leads to migration of antigen-specific T-cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Processing and presentation of myelin-derived peptides by mBECs specifically leads to migration of antigen-specific T-cells.
source: However, when mBECs were loaded with myelin, a significant increase in migrated Th1 and Th17 cells was observed, demonstrating that processing and presentation of myelin-derived peptides by mBECs specifically leads to migration of antigen-specific T-cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Addition of an MHC-II-blocking antibody during the migration period significantly reduced the trans-migration of both Th1 and Th17 cells.
source: Addition of an MHC-II-blocking antibody during the migration period significantly reduced the trans-migration of both Th1 and Th17 cells (Figure 3D,E), further providing evidence that presentation of myelin-derived antigens in MHC-II by mBECs facilitates T-cell migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Presentation of myelin-derived antigens in MHC-II by mBECs facilitates T-cell migration.
source: Addition of an MHC-II-blocking antibody during the migration period significantly reduced the trans-migration of both Th1 and Th17 cells (Figure 3D,E), further providing evidence that presentation of myelin-derived antigens in MHC-II by mBECs facilitates T-cell migration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Using the nominal epitope for 2D2 T-cells (i.e. MOG35–55) to load mBECs with, similar results were obtained as with myelin-loaded mBECs.
source: Using the nominal epitope for 2D2 T-cells (i.e. MOG35–55) to load mBECs with, similar results were obtained as with myelin-loaded mBECs (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: OVA-specific Th1 and Th17 only trans-migrated when encountering OVA-loaded BECs and not when co-cultured with MOG35–55-loaded or medium control BECs.
source: Moreover, our observation that OVA-specific Th1 and Th17 only trans-migrated when encountering OVA-loaded BECs and not when co-cultured with MOG35–55-loaded or medium control BECs substantiates the finding that T-cell migration over the BEC monolayer occurs in an antigen-specific manner (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: T-cell migration over the BEC monolayer occurs in an antigen-specific manner.
source: Moreover, our observation that OVA-specific Th1 and Th17 only trans-migrated when encountering OVA-loaded BECs and not when co-cultured with MOG35–55-loaded or medium control BECs substantiates the finding that T-cell migration over the BEC monolayer occurs in an antigen-specific manner (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: Brain endothelial cells can internalize antigen and promote antigen-specific T cell transmigration in vitro.
source: These data demonstrate that brain endothelial cells can internalize antigen and promote antigen-specific T cell transmigration in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Mice lacking a functional class-II restricted antigen processing machinery are resistant to both active and adoptive transfer EAE.
source: Mice lacking a functional class-II restricted antigen processing machinery are resistant to both active and adoptive transfer EAE (Tompkins et al., 2002), suggesting that proper processing of antigens is essential for disease initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tompkins et al., 2002.

claim: Proper processing of antigens is essential for disease initiation in EAE.
source: Mice lacking a functional class-II restricted antigen processing machinery are resistant to both active and adoptive transfer EAE (Tompkins et al., 2002), suggesting that proper processing of antigens is essential for disease initiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the citation to Tompkins et al., 2002.

claim: Antigen-presentation by the brain endothelium facilitates the entry of antigen-specific CD4+ effector T cells into the brain.
source: Thus, together with our novel data, it seems likely that antigen-presentation by the brain endothelium facilitates the entry of antigen-specific CD4+ effector T cells into the brain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and prior studies discussed.

claim: In Type 1 Diabetes, pancreatic islet antigen expression was shown to be a key factor in governing the ability of the autoantigen-specific T-cells to accumulate in the pancreatic islets.
source: In Type 1 Diabetes, pancreatic islet antigen expression was shown to be a key factor in governing the ability of the autoantigen-specific T-cells to accumulate in the pancreatic islets (Hamilton-Williams et al., 2003; Van Halteren et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hamilton-Williams et al., 2003 and Van Halteren et al., 2005.

claim: Using human T-cell clones and humanized mice, it was demonstrated that only beta cell-specific T-cells reached the pancreatic islets where they destroyed the insulin-producing beta cells.
source: Importantly, using human T-cell clones and humanized mice, it was demonstrated that only beta cell-specific T-cells reached the pancreatic islets where they destroyed the insulin-producing beta cells.
evidence: This claim is based on prior studies, as indicated by the context referencing Unger et al., 2012.

claim: Diabetes unrelated T-cells retained at the peri-vascular sites.
source: By contrast, diabetes unrelated T-cells retained at the peri-vascular sites (Unger et al., 2012), demonstrating that beta-cell-specific T-cells, present in the circulation, need to cross the endothelium to access the pancreatic islets.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Unger et al., 2012.

claim: Beta-cell-specific T-cells, present in the circulation, need to cross the endothelium to access the pancreatic islets.
source: By contrast, diabetes unrelated T-cells retained at the peri-vascular sites (Unger et al., 2012), demonstrating that beta-cell-specific T-cells, present in the circulation, need to cross the endothelium to access the pancreatic islets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the citation to Unger et al., 2012.

claim: The entry of encephalitogenic T-cells into the brain has been shown to pave the way for non-CNS-specific T-cells.
source: The entry of encephalitogenic T-cells into the brain has been shown to pave the way for non-CNS-specific T-cells (Lees et al., 2010; Ludowyk et al., 1992) yet the latter subset remained in an inactive state.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lees et al., 2010 and Ludowyk et al., 1992.

claim: Non-CNS-specific T-cells that enter the brain following encephalitogenic T-cells remained in an inactive state.
source: The entry of encephalitogenic T-cells into the brain has been shown to pave the way for non-CNS-specific T-cells (Lees et al., 2010; Ludowyk et al., 1992) yet the latter subset remained in an inactive state.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lees et al., 2010 and Ludowyk et al., 1992.

claim: Myelin enters the endosomal/lysosomal pathway when internalized by BECs, irrespective of their activation status.
source: Together, the data presented in this study demonstrate for the first time that myelin enters the endosomal/lysosomal pathway when internalized by BECs, irrespective of their activation status.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Dendritic cells mainly internalize antigens being in an immature state.
source: This observation is also different to findings on professional APCs such as dendritic cells, which mainly internalize antigens being in an immature state.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dendritic cells.

claim: BECs maintain to internalize and process exogenous antigens in an activated state.
source: The fact that BECs maintain to internalize and process exogenous antigens in an activated state is advantageous during infection-induced inflammation in the brain (e.g. meningitis) as it will facilitate the presence of antigen-specific effector T-cells to resolve the unwanted infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The continuous facilitation of immune cell entry into the CNS by BECs is destructive in case of MS.
source: However, this continuous facilitation of immune cell entry into the CNS is destructive in case of MS.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings of the study.

claim: BECs can take up and process myelin particles in a time-dependent manner.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that BECs can take up and process myelin particles in a time-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Uptake of myelin, consisting of large particles, by brain endothelial cells predominantly occurs via phagocytosis.
source: Although the focus of the present study was to examine whether antigen-presentation by BECs contributes to transmigration of myelin-reactive T cells, it can be speculated that uptake of myelin, consisting of large particles, by brain endothelial cells predominantly occurs via phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the nature of myelin particles.

claim: BECs have been shown to use different endocytosis mechanisms to internalize particles, which is dependent on the size and composition of the particle.
source: BECs have been shown to use different endocytosis mechanisms to internalize particles, which is dependent on the size and composition of the particle (Faille et al., 2012; Falcone et al., 2006; Georgieva et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Faille et al., 2012, Falcone et al., 2006, and Georgieva et al., 2011.

claim: The upregulation of MHC-II expression under inflammatory conditions reinforces the idea of a non-professional antigen presenting cell role for BECs.
source: Furthermore, the upregulation of MHC-II expression under inflammatory conditions reinforces the idea of a non-professional antigen presenting cell role.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Myelin-derived antigens can be presented by brain endothelial cells in MHC-II to antigen-specific T cell subsets, aiding in the diapedesis of these cells in an MHC-II dependent fashion.
source: Although we do not provide direct evidence for processing and presentation of internalized myelin, our data strongly suggest that myelin-derived antigens can be presented by brain endothelial cells in MHC-II to antigen-specific T cell subsets, aiding in the diapedesis of these cells in an MHC-II dependent fashion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The brain endothelium is an active contributor to disease pathogenesis in MS.
source: These results demonstrate that the brain endothelium is an active contributor to disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Increased immune cell trafficking has a detrimental effect in MS disease progression.
source: Furthermore, these findings have major implications in neuro-inflammatory disorders such as MS, since increased immune cell trafficking has a detrimental effect in disease progression.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MS pathogenesis.

claim: Therapies directed at antigen processing and presentation by BECs could be effective to dampen unwanted immune cell infiltration in MS.
source: Therapies directed at antigen processing and presentation by BECs could be effective to dampen unwanted immune cell infiltration in MS.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings of the study.
